- Age: 9 months  
- Rash onset: 2 days ago, starting on trunk and spreading to arms/legs  
- Morphology: Maculopapular, blanching on pressure (no petechiae/purpura)  
- Systemic features: Afebrile (37.2°C), no irritability, normal feeding, no mucosal lesions  
- Vital signs: HR 120/min (mild, age-expected tachycardia), RR appropriate for age, afebrile  
- General appearance & hydration: Normal  
- Absence of red flags: No conjunctivitis, lip changes, extremity edema/erythema, cervical lymphadenopathy, or respiratory/gastrointestinal symptoms

- Reassurance: Self-limited course; typically resolves within 3–7 days  
- Symptomatic care only (e.g., gentle skin care; no antihistamines or topical steroids needed)  
- Counsel caregivers to monitor for emergence of fever, lethargy, poor feeding, or rash non-blanching — though risk is exceedingly low given current presentation  
- No laboratory testing or imaging indicated

This is a classic presentation of a benign, self-limited viral exanthem in an immunocompetent infant. - Rash onset 2 days ago, starting on trunk and spreading to arms/legs — classic centrifugal pattern of viral exanthems  
- Maculopapular morphology — common in enteroviral and other benign viral rashes  
- Rash blanches on pressure and lacks petechiae/purpura — excludes vasculitis, meningococcemia, and thrombocytopenic causes  
- Afebrile (37.2°C) — argues strongly against acute bacterial infection, Kawasaki disease, or systemic viral illness like measles or EBV  
- No irritability, normal feeding, normal hydration — indicates absence of significant systemic toxicity  
- No mucosal lesions, conjunctivitis, lip changes, extremity edema/erythema, or cervical lymphadenopathy — excludes Kawasaki disease, scarlet fever, Stevens-Johnson syndrome, and infectious mononucleosis  
- No respiratory or gastrointestinal symptoms — reduces likelihood of atypical presentations of more severe infections  
- Normal general appearance and vital signs otherwise appropriate for age — supports benign course  

[GAPS]  
- No viral testing (e.g., PCR for enterovirus in stool or throat) — but not clinically indicated or necessary for diagnosis  
- No detailed medication or exposure history (e.g., new foods, topicals, antibiotics) — though absence of suggestive features makes drug eruption highly unlikely  
- No family or daycare exposure history — supportive but not required for diagnosis  
None  

[DIAGNOSIS]  
Benign viral exanthem (enteroviral)
